lead: Space vector modulation (SVM or SVPWM) treats the three legs of the bridge as one unit. The eight switch states become eight voltage vectors: six active vectors 60° apart and two zero vectors. The wanted three-phase output is one vector rotating at the output frequency, and in every switching period the modulator makes it on average from the two nearest active vectors and the zero vectors. SVM uses the bus 15.5 % better than plain sine-triangle PWM and is easy to code, so most three-phase drives and grid inverters use it.
prereq: You need: the six-switch bridge from 180° and 120° conduction and the linear limit of sinusoidal PWM.

sections.h3: Eight states and the space vector

blocks.text: Write S<sub>a</sub> = 1 when the top switch of leg a is on and 0 when the bottom one is. The state (S<sub>a</sub> S<sub>b</sub> S<sub>c</sub>) takes eight values. In 000 and 111 all three terminals are on one rail, so the load voltage is zero: these are the zero vectors V0 and V7. The other six, 100, 110, 010, 011, 001 and 101, are the active vectors V1 to V6.

Three phase voltages that add to zero can be drawn as one vector in a plane with axes α (along phase a) and β (90° ahead). The Clarke transform with the 2/3 scale keeps the vector length equal to the phase peak:
vα = (2/3)(va − vb/2 − vc/2) and vβ = (vb − vc)/√3. State 100 gives star-load phase voltages 2Vdc/3, −Vdc/3, −Vdc/3, so vα = 2Vdc/3 and vβ = 0.

So every active vector is 2V<sub>dc</sub>/3 long. The six tips form a hexagon, the zero vectors sit at its centre, and the six triangles between neighbouring vectors are sectors 1 to 6. A balanced sine output of phase peak V<sub>m</sub> is a reference vector V<sub>ref</sub> of length V<sub>m</sub> turning at ω = 2πf.

In each switching period T<sub>s</sub> the modulator applies the two active vectors that bound the sector, here called V<sub>x</sub> (the one at the start of the sector) and V<sub>y</sub> (the next one), for times T<sub>x</sub> and T<sub>y</sub>, and the zero vectors for the rest, T<sub>0</sub>. The volt-seconds must match:
Vref Ts = Vx Tx + Vy Ty with T0 = Ts − Tx − Ty spent on V0 and V7, which add nothing.
Tx = m Ts sin(60° − θ), Ty = m Ts sin θ θ is the reference angle measured from Vx (0° to 60°), m = √3 Vm/Vdc is the modulation index and Ts the switching period.

T<sub>x</sub> + T<sub>y</sub> = m T<sub>s</sub> cos(30° − θ) is largest at θ = 30°, where it equals m T<sub>s</sub>. So the linear range is m ≤ 1, a phase peak of V<sub>dc</sub>/√3 = 0.577V<sub>dc</sub>. Sine-triangle PWM stops at V<sub>dc</sub>/2, so SVM gives 2/√3 = 1.155 times more, a line voltage of up to 0.707V<sub>dc</sub> rms. Some books define the index as V<sub>m</sub>/(V<sub>dc</sub>/2) instead; then the SVM limit is 1.155.

The zero time is split equally between V0 and V7, and the period is arranged so that only one leg changes at each step. In sector 1 the seven-segment sequence is 000 → 100 → 110 → 111 → 110 → 100 → 000, spending T<sub>0</sub>/4, T<sub>x</sub>/2, T<sub>y</sub>/2, T<sub>0</sub>/2, T<sub>y</sub>/2, T<sub>x</sub>/2, T<sub>0</sub>/4. Each leg switches on once and off once per period, and the pattern is symmetric about the centre, which lowers current ripple.

Each leg is on for the sum of the segments in which its bit is 1. In sector 1 leg a is on for T<sub>x</sub> + T<sub>y</sub> + T<sub>0</sub>/2, leg b for T<sub>y</sub> + T<sub>0</sub>/2 and leg c for T<sub>0</sub>/2. These three times go straight into the compare registers of a microcontroller timer. The result equals sine-triangle PWM with a common-mode term −(max + min)/2 added to the references; it cancels in the line voltages.

figure.caption: The six active vectors, each 2V<sub>dc</sub>/3 = 400 V long on the 600 V bus, form a hexagon with the zero vectors at its centre. The worked example’s 300 V reference at 20° in sector 1 is made from 92.8 μs of V1 and 49.4 μs of V2 in each 166.7 μs period; the dashed circle is the 346.4 V linear limit.

spec.aria: A hexagon with six vectors V1 to V6 labelled with their switch states, sectors 1 to 6 between them, and the zero vectors at the centre. A reference vector of 300 volts at 20 degrees is drawn as the sum of a part along V1 and a part along V2. A box lists the dwell times 92.8, 49.4 and 24.5 microseconds.

examples.question: A three-phase VSI has V<sub>dc</sub> = 600 V and switches at 6 kHz. The wanted phase voltage peak is V<sub>m</sub> = 300 V, and at one instant the reference is in sector 1 at θ = 20°. Find m, T<sub>x</sub>, T<sub>y</sub> and T<sub>0</sub>, check the linear range, and give the on-time of each leg.
steps: Linear limit V<sub>dc</sub>/√3 = 346.4 V; 300 V is below it, so m < 1.
T<sub>0</sub> = 166.7 − 92.8 − 49.4 = 24.5 μs: 12.26 μs of V7 in the middle and 6.13 μs of V0 at each end.
Leg a: T<sub>x</sub> + T<sub>y</sub> + T<sub>0</sub>/2 = 154.4 μs; leg b: T<sub>y</sub> + T<sub>0</sub>/2 = 61.6 μs; leg c: T<sub>0</sub>/2 = 12.3 μs.
examples.answer: m = 0.866; T<sub>x</sub> = 92.8 μs, T<sub>y</sub> = 49.4 μs, T<sub>0</sub> = 24.5 μs; legs a, b, c on for 154.4, 61.6 and 12.3 μs of each 166.7 μs.

examples.question: A drive on a 400 V bus switching at 10 kHz must give 230 V rms line to line. At one instant the reference angle is α = 200°. Find m, the sector, θ, the dwell times, the switching sequence and the leg on-times.
steps: Sector = floor(200/60) + 1 = 4; θ = 200 − 180 = 20°. In sector 4, V<sub>x</sub> = V4 (011) and V<sub>y</sub> = V5 (001).
Leg a is on only in 111: 9.96 μs. Leg b is on in 011 and 111: T<sub>x</sub> + T<sub>0</sub>/2 = 62.23 μs. Leg c is on in 001, 011 and 111: 90.04 μs.
Check: the bus allows 282.8 V rms with SVM; plain SPWM would allow only 245.0 V and need m<sub>a</sub> = 0.939.
examples.answer: m = 0.813; sector 4, θ = 20°; T<sub>x</sub> = 52.27 μs, T<sub>y</sub> = 27.81 μs, T<sub>0</sub> = 19.92 μs; legs a, b, c on for 9.96, 62.23 and 90.04 μs.

traps: Each active vector is 2V<sub>dc</sub>/3 long, not V<sub>dc</sub>/2 or V<sub>dc</sub>.
θ in the dwell-time formulas is measured from the start of the sector, not from the α axis.
V<sub>x</sub> and V<sub>y</sub> are the two vectors bounding the sector the reference is in; in sector 4 they are V4 and V5, not V1 and V2.
T<sub>0</sub> is spent in both zero states, 000 and 111, not as "all switches off".
The SVM linear limit is a phase peak of V<sub>dc</sub>/√3, not V<sub>dc</sub>/2 (that is sine-triangle PWM).

quiz.q: List the eight switch states of a three-phase VSI and name the zero vectors.
Why can SVM give a phase peak of V<sub>dc</sub>/√3 when each active vector is 2V<sub>dc</sub>/3 long?
quiz.a: The reference must stay inside the circle that fits in the hexagon. Its radius is the distance to the middle of a side, (2V<sub>dc</sub>/3) cos 30° = V<sub>dc</sub>/√3, so that is the largest |V<sub>ref</sub>| = V<sub>m</sub>.

quiz.q: V<sub>dc</sub> = 500 V, V<sub>m</sub> = 200 V, T<sub>s</sub> = 100 μs and θ = 30°. Find m, T<sub>x</sub>, T<sub>y</sub> and T<sub>0</sub>.
A reference is at α = 135°. Find the sector, θ and the two active vectors.
Why does SVM use both zero states in one period instead of only 000?
quiz.a: With 000 at the ends and 111 in the middle, every step changes one leg only, so each leg switches twice per period. Using only 000 would force extra transitions.

SVM gives 15.5 % more line voltage (0.707V<sub>dc</sub> against 0.612V<sub>dc</sub> rms) and lower current ripple at the same switching frequency; it is computed per period from the sector and angle. SPWM needs only comparators; with a min-max common-mode term added it gives the same pulses as SVM.

beyond: Not for the exam. Field-oriented drives feed SVM from the current controllers, and overmodulation schemes extend it up to six-step. Discontinuous SVM uses only one zero vector per sector to cut switching loss by a third. Search for SVPWM overmodulation and discontinuous space vector PWM.
